newsitem.title: UK: Discreet FX intervention reaps rewards in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Discreet FX intervention reaps rewards in Europe.

text.p: European central banks have learnt discretion is the better part of valour when it comes to intervening to keep their currencies stable in the European exchange rate mechanism.

The most successful, like the Bank of France, have abandoned high-profile intervention in favour of discreet buying and selling to trap their currencies in tight bands around their central ERM parities against the mark.

Standing ready to intervene without drawing obvious lines in the sand for the market to challenge has paid rich rewards: even the turmoil triggered by the French elections and last week's row between the Bundesbank and Bonn failed to jolt EMS currencies too much.

"The Bank of France and the Bank of Spain are the most inclined to intervene in Europe and are the most committed to currency stability," said Philippa Malmgren, the European currency strategist at Bankers Trust.

"It is typical of them to do it one way or the other, and people have learnt the mark/French cross is the last one they would want to attack," she said. "Even a dispute between the Bundesbank and the government and the elections in France weren't enough to make people challenge the link between the mark and the franc."

The franc has stayed stubbornly within one percent of its central ERM parity of 3.3539 marks so far this year and held within the 2.25 percent ERM bands that existed until 1993 since early September 1996.

This has kept one-month mark/Paris volatility near historic lows. One-month mark/French franc volatility rose to no more than 3.10/3.60 percent when concern about the outlook for EMU was at its zenith last week and snapped back to 1.5/2.0 percent Tuesday.
With almost 90 percent of French notes and bonds held by domestic investors, speculators have had a hard time whipping up a run on the franc.
The Bank of France has made it even harder by shrouding its intervention with an air of mystery.

"You don't usually see the BOF in but the names executing the buy orders are the ones that usually execute orders on behalf of the BOF and that keeps everyone wary," said a trader at a UK bank in London.
Purchases of French notes and bonds by state-owned institutions at key junctures has also led some traders to speculate about the French monetary authorities' involvement.
Other European central banks have been equally zealous at keeping their currencies orbiting close to their central mark parity in the ERM.
The Bank of Finland bought marks for markkaa Tuesday, traders said, as the Finnish currency extended gains above its central ERM parity rate of 3.04 per mark.
The Bank of Spain was reported by traders to be buying pesetas for marks last week and was equally actively selling it earlier this year when it was rising against the mark.
"Central banks have learnt a lot from the last few years," said Avinash Persaud, the currency strategist at JP Morgan. "The perception of stability leads to further stability."
And this seems to be just what European central banks have engineered in the run up to the launch of the European single currency, when stability in the EMS will be a factor in deciding who joins.
